title: Second Smallest in Min-Tree
statement:
You are given a **perfect binary tree** (every internal node has two children and all leaves are on the same level) in which **every node stores the smallest value of the subtree rooted at it**. Equivalently, each internal node equals the minimum of its two children, so each internal value is a copy of some leaf value. All leaf values are distinct, and the tree has at least two leaves.

Find the **second smallest distinct value** stored in the whole tree.

The tree is stored as an array in heap order: `tree[0]` is the root and the children of `tree[i]` are `tree[2i + 1]` and `tree[2i + 2]`. The interviewer wanted a solution that takes `O(log n)` time by using the structure of the tree instead of scanning every node. (Reading the input is `O(n)` regardless; the complexity below refers to the work done on the tree.)
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`, the number of nodes.
The second line contains `n` integers `tree[0] ... tree[n-1]`.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the second smallest distinct value in the tree.
constraints: 3 ≤ n ≤ 131071, and n = 2^h - 1 for some h ≥ 2
Every internal node equals the minimum of its two children

examples.explanation: The leaves are `8 3 6 5`, so the root is 3. The second smallest value must have lost a comparison directly against 3: along the path of the 3 the losers are 8 (at the bottom) and 5 (on the other side of the root). The smaller of them is 5.
The root is 4 and its only competitor is the other leaf, 7.
The minimum 9 travels from a leaf to the root through the right subtree. The values it beat along the way are 40, 12 and 11; the smallest of these, 11, is the second smallest value.

hints: The root is the minimum. The second smallest value must be a leaf that was eliminated directly by the minimum in some comparison, like the runner-up of a knockout tournament.
Start at the root and follow the child whose value equals the root's value. The sibling you did not follow is a candidate for the answer.
Repeat down to a leaf: that is only log n candidates. The answer is the smallest candidate.
